title: How does an octopus find food in the dark?
hook: In flowing water, food leaves an invisible trail. Can an octopus follow it?
paper_title: Octopus track chemosensory plumes to find food
summary: In dark laboratory flumes, red octopuses preferentially approached food upstream and from within an estimated chemical plume. Movement patterns suggest that arms and suckers may help guide search.
evidence_note: Repeated successful approaches, small laboratory samples, estimated plume and no isolated sensory-organ manipulation limit the inference.

evidence.design: Five O. rubescens in repeated three-station trials; separate one-station task analyzed five males after four exclusions; 41 successful approaches. Blackout tent, near-infrared recording, flowing water; estimated plume from proxy-bead visualization.

claims.claim: In dark flowing water, successful upstream approaches favored baited over empty stations.
claims.location: Materials and methods, Three-station discrimination task; Results and Figure 4.

claims.claim: Thirty-one of 41 successful feeding approaches arrived from within the approximate plume; ten from outside.
Pauses, turns, upstream surges and more fast arm-aligned movements occurred during tracking than controls.

limitations: Repeated events are not independent animals; only successful feeding events are counted.
Five analyzed males in single-station task; four excluded for presumed low appetite.
Plume geometry was estimated using proxy particles rather than directly measuring the actual cue at each animal.
Suckers are a plausible sensory guide, not an experimentally isolated mechanism.
Laboratory conditions do not demonstrate wild foraging distances or a universal search strategy.

A separate test recorded forty-one successful approaches by five males. Thirty-one arrived from inside the estimated chemical plume.
They paused, zigzagged and surged upstream.

posts.caption:
How does an octopus find food without visible light? In dark laboratory flumes, East Pacific red octopuses favored baited stations when approaching upstream. In a separate task, 31 of 41 successful approaches by five analyzed males arrived from inside the estimated chemical plume. These are repeated feeding events, not 41 animals. Suckers might help guide the search, but the experiment did not isolate the sensory organs. Small samples, excluded animals and a proxy plume limit generalization.

Weertman et al. (2025), PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0330262
Full text: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12507230/
Evidence and credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-012.html
